Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I received in my mail yesterday, too late to bring to the attention of this house, an envelope bearing the frank "W.D.H., M.P." In this envelope there was no letter from a member of the House of Commons, but a press release and communication from Mr. George North, who is the editor of The Fisherman, a weekly newspaper published in Vancouver for fishermen and known by everyone in Vancouver to be a communist slanted paper. In the accompanying note he says to me:
Dear Mr. Deachman:
Thought you might be interested in the accompanying statement issued June 7 in regard to Norpac treaty negotiations.
With that he enclosed his press release, which has some pretty disparaging things to say about the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) and those associated with him. I will quote from it briefly:
Only a man who is deaf-
He refers here to the Minister of Fisheries:
-dumb and blind could have failed to realize that this was no threat but a logical move on the part of the Japanese to take advantage of the weak kneed-
He spells that "need":
-unprincipled approach to these problems displayed by the Canadian government, its fisheries department and its hand picked puppets.
Then he goes on a little later to say:
He can either continue to evade and dodge the facts of life and mislead the people of Canada whom he professes to represent and supinely knuckle down to the U.S. state department or he can stand up for the fishermen-
My question of privilege is this. Can a member of the House of Commons give the stationery of the House of Commons and his frank to someone outside the house for the purpose of disseminating material of this kind, without any accompanying note, explanation or covering memorandum from that member?

MR. OLSON    REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, which arises out of an answer that I received from the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour on June 3. On that date the parliamentary secretary answered a question I had on the order paper, and I should like to read both the question and the reply so that you, sir, together with other hon. members, will be able to understand the question of privilege I am raising. They are as follows:
Has representation been received from any of the provinces to extend the 75 per cent rate of

Question of Privilege
reimbursement to the provinces with respect to approved capital costs for building and equipment purchased within the agreement of federal-provincial technical and vocational training schools?
The answer given was "Yes".
The third part of the same question is as follows:
Is the government considering increasing the federal share of cost of operation in the vocational training section of these schools?
The answer given to me, Mr. Speaker, was "No". Yesterday the Minister of Labour in his statement to the house had this to say:
In order to step up the training of unemployed workers of all ages the government will introduce an amendment to the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act to increase the contribution to the provinces of the cost of provincial training allowances to unemployed persons from 75 per cent to 90 per cent.
A second point in the statement the minister made yesterday was to the effect that the government intended to increase from 50 per cent to 75 per cent the federal contribution to the cost of retraining employed workers.
I do not question the right of a minister or a parliamentary secretary to say, for example, that a question is under review, or that it is under active review, or that the government will announce its policy in due course. I would suggest, however, that an unqualified "no" in these circumstances is not reliable, and that either the parliamentary secretary did not communicate with the Minister of Labour or else he gave me a false answer. As I have said, I do not contend that any minister has to give an immediate reply to a question, but I do not believe he should give a wrong answer. So I am suggesting that the Minister of Labour should get together with his parliamentary secretary before answers are given to these questions.
I am not interested in whether or not the parliamentary secretary wishes to apologize for having given me this wrong answer, but I do think we should have an assurance from him that the answers he does give to these questions are to be relied on.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: MR. OLSON    REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
The answers which were given by the parliamentary secretary were seen by myself and approved. Therefore, I certainly want to take upon myself any responsibility attaching to the answer given to the hon. member. Unfortunately, as he developed his question of privilege the hon. gentleman did not refer to the particular question he had in mind, so I was not able to follow him. I shall be glad to compare the answers given to his question with the statement which was made yesterday, and it may be that the apparent contradiction which the hon. member feels

exists will disappear on further examination. However, I shall be glad to look at this and deal with it tomorrow.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to promote increased employment in Canada by the provision of financial assistance by way of loans to municipalities, the object of such loans being to enable municipalities to augment or accelerate their capital works program subject to the approval of the provinces concerned; and for this purpose to provide a special fund in the consolidated revenue fund not exceeding four hundred million dollars to be available for the making of loans to municipalities and certain other municipal authorities for specific municipal capital works projects; to establish a municipal development and loan board to administer the fund so provided; to authorize the acceptance of municipal debentures for any loans so made; to authorize a measure of forgiveness in respect of any loans so made, depending upon the date of completion of the projects for which such loans are made; and to provide further for other related and incidental matters.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
It is with considerable pleasure that I rise to move the resolution concerning the municipal development and loan act. I should like to make a brief statement at this time and give a broad outline of the provisions of the proposed legislation. Members of this committee are aware of this government's determination to do everything possible to combat serious unemployment in this country. One of the constructive ways in which this can be done is by assisting municipalities to proceed with needed capital works, many of which have been long deferred, and to help them expand and accelerate current programs.
Over the past five years, as has already been stated, an annual average of 6.6 per cent of our working force has been unemployed. This meant that on the average 425 thousand Canadians were without work during each of those years. At the same time countless essential municipal works were crying out to be undertaken. These are works which could offer employment to thousands of our citizens while benefiting hundreds of
[Mr. Fairweather.l
thousands with permanent community facilities. It is this situation that the municipal development and loan act is designed to meet.
In essence, the proposed act seeks to increase employment by the creation of new jobs in the construction industry engaged in municipal capital projects. The construction industry in Canada is particularly suited to employing large numbers of persons who currently make up the ranks of our unemployed. Many without work today have relatively few skills. Some of these are Canadians born from farms who have moved into urban communities. Many are newcomers to Canada facing difficulty in establishing their families here. Others, again, need work for short periods of time, particularly during the winter months when the construction industry could operate at higher capacity if the demand for buildings and capital facilities were expanded and maintained throughout the year.
As I have indicated, one of the primary purposes of the proposed bill is to help expand the construction of basic community facilities in order to increase employment. The effectiveness of this program should be increased materially by virtue of the fact that most municipalities from one end of the country to the other have developmental projects which they could bring forward provided financial assistance is made available. Thus the employment effects should be as widespread as it is possible to ensure. Moreover, it should be possible, and it is the government's hope that it does prove possible, to get on with many projects during the coming winter months.
As indicated in the resolution, the bill will provide loans to municipalities by the federal government up to an authorized limit of $400 million. Loans under this program will be available for a period of nearly three years ending March 31, 1966. The bill will provide further that one quarter of the amount of each loan may be forgiven on work on eligible projects completed on or before March 31, 1966.
Forgiveness of a significant portion of each loan is, of course, not only an incentive to municipalities to proceed quickly with eligible projects. It is equally important in helping to hold down the size and burden of long term debt and to lower the carrying charges on the net balance of the loan.
Loans under the bill will be extended only with the express approval of the provincial authorities. Speaking in Toronto on May 29 to the federation of mayors and municipalities, the Prime Minister emphasized that financial assistance will be given in ways which fully

observe both the spirit and letter of the constitution. The bill we propose to introduce fulfils that undertaking. It provides that loans may be made only after a municipality has secured explicit provincial approval for eligible projects and for related borrowing by way of debentures. The operating procedures proposed are equally consistent, we believe, with full respect for the constitution which places the municipalities under the sole and exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
The intent of the proposed legislation is that loans will be available to assist financing of important and useful projects when they represent additions to, or acceleration of, capital programs which municipalities would otherwise have carried out. It is not the purpose of the federal government to act as a lender of last resort to the municipalities. The primary intention of this bill is to provide the maximum number of new jobs in this area over a relatively short time.
Municipal projects eligible for financing through these loans will be limited to the kinds of capital works listed in the bill. These capital works cover the main facilities and services of a municipality. The list is limited to avoid overlapping with other programs, such as assistance to sewer construction already provided through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, or existing federal grants for hospital construction. It is limited also to avoid infringing the exclusive provincial jurisdiction over education. However, the eligible list will enable approximately one half of the capital expenditures for which municipalities normally borrow to qualify under the bill.
Loans will cover two thirds of the approved cost of eligible projects. The rate of interest will be based on the government's own long term borrowing rate, and it will thus be considerably lower than the rate at which most municipalities themselves could borrow. At the same time the real cost to municipalities of funds advanced under the bill will be reduced to a very low level by the forgiveness feature it contains.
It is expected that the proposed authorization of $400 million will meet the potential demand for loans for additional projects of an eligible kind. When it is considered that loans are applied to two thirds of project cost, it is evident that if full use is made of the program $400 million in loans will provide the base for a minimum of $600 million of additional projects over the period of the program. This would represent an increase of nearly 50 per cent in the capital expenditures by municipalities on projects eligible for loans. It would represent an increase of nearly 25 per cent in over-all capital spending by municipalities during the loan period.
11.	1963	889
Municipal Development and Loan Board
The achievement of a program of this magnitude, based on loans totalling $400 million by the federal government, will make a major contribution to new employment, and at the same time will result in a marked increase in community facilities. The administration of the new program will be carried out by a loan board working in the closest collaboration with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, whose activities place it in close touch with municipalities and their problems.
The bill provides that a service agreement may be arranged between the new loan board and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation whereby the latter will use its facilities, field offices and personnel to assist the board with the loan program. This will enable the board to start its operations quickly and at the same time avoid building up a new organization which would duplicate many of the services already available through C.M.H.C. While it is contemplated that C.M.H.C. will provide many of the administrative services under the act, the prime initiative for developing the loan program will remain with the loan board. The responsibility for decisions with respect to loans and for the administration of the act will rest with the board. The board itself will report to my colleague the Minister of National Revenue, who is the minister responsible for the operations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The new program will be in addition to the various ways in which the government is already assisting, or planning to assist, the municipalities. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned yesterday, I think it was, when talking about the winter works program, this program, to use his phrase, will be dovetailed with the other programs designed to create work throughout the country through the winter months and throughout the year. This program will not displace existing programs. In fact it will serve to reinforce them by increasing the financial resources for municipal capital investment.
Mr. Chairman, I am looking forward to giving a fuller explanation of the provisions of the bill at the appropriate stage of its consideration by the house. I trust this consideration will make clear to hon. members of the committee and to the country the material contribution which the proposed loan program can make to the solution of our unemployment problem. This is a matter of great concern to all hon. members, and I ask for their co-operation in expediting the passage of the proposed legislation so that it may begin to be effective during the coming winter.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this time I intend to refer generally to some of the matters to which reference has been made by the Minister of Finance. He has chosen to refer in some detail to the provisions of the bill which will be introduced. That, of course, should not be done in discussion of a resolution, because the bill is not before the committee and no reference regarding its particulars should be made.
However, I would say immediately that this plan will be examined with care and attention on the part of the opposition. It is going to bring about the expenditure, in a period of three years, of some $400 million. We have had no indication where that money is coming from or how it is going to be procured. Many of these things, of course, will be made clear when the budget is introduced on Thursday night.

However, I should have thought the minister would have been able to give us some of his views on the question of finance in connection with this matter, views which were, to say the least, considered unorthodox by most members of the house but which received the support of the 16 other hon. gentlemen opposite who today occupy the treasury benches. You will recall, sir, that on November 6, 1962, all Liberal members in the house voted in favour of the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Red Deer, which provided that there should be adopted-I am summarizing-a policy of debt free money. This motion received the support of the present Minister of Finance and, as I said a moment ago, of a host of others who today occupy the seats of government.
What has taken place in the interim? Do they still believe in this principle which they supported then? Did they become converts to the ideas of Social Credit for only two days? These are things I should like the Minister of Finance to explain in order that I may find out when his troubled mind became clear following the writing of "Troubled Canada". Is this, then the means of financing this proposal? We ought to know something about that. I am sure the minister, with his accustomed frankness, will either say that he approved of this unorthodox amendment moved by the leader of the Social Credit party on the basis of political expedience at the time or that, in truth, he had accepted holus-bolus the financial implications of it which are far removed from the background and associations of the hon. gentleman.
I was interested in the speech delivered in Toronto by the Prime Minister when he addressed the Canadian association of mayors and municipalities. At that time he led those representatives to believe, although I am sure it was unintentional, that all kinds and varieties of public institutions could be built by them with these loans, that the sluice gates of credit were being opened to them. These people were led to believe that the policies of the Minister of Finance would make ample credit facilities available, would make interest rates as low as possible, to use words which he used just prior to the election, and that these policies would be carried into effect. Well, the association of mayors certainly approved of what they heard, because they thought vast sums of money were going to be made available to them in the manner requested over a period of years.
I think I could do no better than refer to the brief that was presented by the

municipal governments of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, to the government of which I had the honour to be the head on November 9, 1962. The item to which I shall refer in the brief is under the heading "National monetary loan fund". The federation has recommended the establishment of a municipal loan fund or a municipal development bank. Then I note that the brief refers to the fact that this would help each urban area undertake planned development programs which would not only provide work but would direct such work to the satisfaction of basic community needs.
The principle of the municipal loan fund is already recognized by the federal government in the legislation which authorizes long term financing of trunk sewers and sewage treatment plants. In effect, the federation is urging that federal loans should also be made available for other basic community facilities, for example for urban roads, bridges and mass transit facilities, for the acquisition of property for redevelopment, for water supply and for the purchase of recreation space.
I can only infer, after having listened to the minister, that what the municipalities asked for they are not going to get. The brief called attention to the basic need for long term federal loans on favourable rates of interest in order to finance projects which are primarily self-liquidating and essential to community development, such as urban roads, bridges, transit facilities, sewers, water supply, recreation, land for development, grants on a more adequate scale toward the cost of hospitals, schools, and other community services which are essential but are non-self liquidating.
During the course of the campaign the minister himself made many promises in this connection. He enunciated an eight point program which it is very interesting to read again. First he refers to the need for easy money, ample credit facilities, low interest rates, low interest loans to municipalities for needed public works and services to stimulate the construction industry; low cost loans for municipal public works; low interest loans to create jobs by enabling municipalities to build schools and hospitals, rebuild streets and sidewalks, clear slums, improve transit systems and undertake urban renewal projects. Over and over again he set out this national program. Until we see the bill we will not be able to ascertain the extent to which the promises of a few months ago have been translated into the performance of today.
The general plan of the municipalities was suggested by Mayor Mongrain of Three Rivers. He set out in detail their demands and their requirements. Now, to begin with, we recognized when we were in office that

Municipal Development and Loan Board there were certain fields of national development that would welcome the assistance of the federal government, such as housing, a national problem, and the problem of pollution which is becoming increasingly serious. Indeed, unless we take more and more effective action it will not be long before our vast water resources are poisoned by reason of the pouring in of sewage and industrial wastes resulting in a loss to this and future generations.
There can be no question that many of the matters covered by the hon. gentleman come within the jurisdiction of the provinces. I hear much about what this government intends to do in connection with the constitution. I read that Mr. Lesage, the premier of Quebec, has presented the government of Canada with an ultimatum, an ultimatum so-called by one of his ministers, which is apparently designed to assure that the rights of the provinces shall be respected and maintained. Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, speaking in the latter part of the month of May, predicted an early end to certain joint programs through federal government withdrawal. I want to know what those fields are. Is one of them the winter works program which was laughed at when first introduced but which has provided many jobs for Canadians in every part of Canada?
Why introduce this measure at this time, before the budget? Why the introduction in haphazard form of these various suggestions? Let us see the whole picture rather than having matters presented in a haphazard, piecemeal manner. The Prime Minister today, in purple faced annoyance and rage at a question I asked him regarding the convening of a conference with the provinces, finally answered, after being pressed to do so, that a conference was going to take place. I can understand his annoyance because he is having plenty of trouble with his major supporter, the premier of the province of Quebec. That premier has decided what shall be done by this government and this government has to be very careful that it does not transgress in any way the ultimata that emerge from the legislative buildings in Quebec.
The maintenance of the constitution has always been of the essence of Conservative policy. We have followed that throughout the years. Why has this legislation not been submitted to the provinces? Why has such legislation in general not been placed before the provinces to get their views? Certainly I think that is a very proper question. The provinces are not going to be denied the right to say which projects shall in fact be acceptable. Every project that a municipality

Municipal Development and Loan Board desires to place before the government will have to have the approval of the province within which that project is located.
I say that in view of the changes inherent in this legislation there should be a federal-provincial meeting to review all aspects of municipal finance. Assistance Act, of 1938, the hon. member mentioned that that legislation had been in force for two years but had become inoperative in 1940, when loans had ceased to be granted.
So, as you can see, the Leader of the Opposition himself is interested in the speeches and ideas of the Social Crediters since he saw fit to mention a part of them in his recent speech.
If there is one thing that the Leader of the Opposition should not forget, it is that if he had started before today to put into practice some of the sound, sensible and reasonable ideas that the Social Crediters have been putting forward for many years, he might not sit today where he is but he might still sit on the other side in the house. But it took him such a long time to understand or rather to misunderstand that he had scarcely been five years in power when the opposition parties succeeded in persuading the people that the government had neither fulfilled their promises nor accomplished what was expected of them while they were in power. And the people took it upon themselves to remind him of it, precisely because he had refused to accept as his own some of the sensible and logical ideas of Social Credit. Thus he was sent back into opposition by the people and there he will remain for many years to come if not forever.
For my part, Mr. Chairman, I must say that we are ready to accept this resolution we are discussing now, in the broad outline that has been given and although we were not given the details that we would like to have.
As a matter of fact, Social Crediters have been asking since 1935 that loans be granted to municipalities by the Bank of Canada.
More than ten years ago, the province of Alberta started granting loans to municipalities of that province at interest rates of 2i, 2J and 3 per cent.
Municipal Development and Loan Board accept: the running into debt of a government in order to make loans available to municipalities.
Today, at last, the Liberals are ready to accept that idea. It was just as good 25 years ago, Mr. Chairman. It was just as good 15 and 10 years ago, but today after having heard it stated and explained from every angle, we note that the Minister of Finance in the present government (Mr. Gordon) has deemed it advisable to put it into practice. We do not know much about the details, but just the same, we have a few suggestions to make and we hope that when the bill is introduced in this house, some of those particulars will be included in the bill.
The first point and the most important is this. The Leader of the Opposition said a moment ago: Where will the money come from to lend those $400 million to the municipalities? Where will those $400 million come from? We Social Crediters say: From the Bank of Canada. Why the Bank of Canada? Precisely because the Bank of Canada was set up to meet not only an ever growing development but also the needs of municipal and provincial governments as well as those of the Canadian people as a whole. The Bank of Canada could finance those $400 million at administrative cost. Being an excellent accountant, the Minister of Finance will realize that this is no inflationary policy for this country. Any accountant who does a company's bookkeeping uses the double entry system, with all the assets in one column and the liabilities in the other.
When the Bank of Canada creates the required credit, it will be added to the accruing assets of this country.
Supposing, for instance, that the Bank of Canada loans an amount to the city of Montreal to finance the building of a subway about which there has been so much talk for
At our national convention in July 1961, when Social Crediters laid down their policies and their program, an item of that program suggested precisely that the Bank of Canada should grant loans without interest to municipalities.
During the last session, in 1962, the leader of the New Democratic party, the first to be won over to such an idea, advocated the granting of loans to municipalities by the federal government. He did not mention the Bank of Canada, however, but he felt that those loans could be made available through the constant running into debt of the federal government. This is something we could not 28902-5-57J
so many years; whenever a new section is built, it will mean a new asset on the credit side of this country, if the Bank of Canada grants new credit to balance the added assets, we will only have some sound accounting, as any good accountant will appreciate. Then, the Minister of Finance will not be able to' criticize what we are claiming today.
Whenever new assets are added to a country s credit, whether it be a subway, bridges, schools, municipal filtration plants^ etc., the Bank of Canada should create new credit as those assets are developed. It is a normal thing, because the municipalities are in return asked to repay the loans as the

Municipal Development and Loan Board municipal buildings depreciate. For instance if a subway is supposed to last 100 years and costs $200 million, $2 million a year should be asked, and, in a hundred years, when it is completely depreciated, and it is time to rebuild it, the subway will be completely paid for.
Such a system means that, as new riches are added to the country's assets, by erecting new buildings, or building new municipal roads, the Bank of Canada should put out new credit, and as everything depreciates, the bank will ask for reimbursement, which means that, at any time, circulating credit is about the same, neither larger nor smaller, but equal to the country's wealth, that is to the social capital of the country, to be written on the credit side of the municipalities and provinces.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the first suggestion. That, Mr. Chairman, was the first suggestion we made to the Minister of Finance. He should finance those $400 million through the Bank of Canada and then we would not have any misgivings about the centralizing or autonomist ideas of this government, because then the Bank of Canada would become the organization charged with community development financing, not the federal government. It would be the Bank of Canada which in fact would be also the federal government bank as much as the provincial government bank, but above all the bank of the Canadian people, since it would not be only the creature of the federal government but above all of the public bodies and all the government organizations both federal and provincial.
Then nobody would be able to blame the federal government for interfering because it would not be the federal government who would enter the field of municipal development, but it would be the Bank of Canada which would grant assistance to the provinces in order that they be in a position to pass that assistance on to the municipalities.
Mr. Chairman, it would certainly help remedy unemployment if the Bank of Canada created new credit. A moment ago I heard the minister when he said that one of the purposes of this bill was to fight unemployment. Now, this new fund will assist the municipalities to carry out capital projects which would create new jobs. This is how we could check unemployment, because this would not be a creation of new jobs to increase production of goods but it would rather be new jobs in the field of public works which would contribute to increase the wealth of this country and the wealth 

that would not be saleable in an immediate or far-off future, but public wealth.
Every time we increase our public works, we increase the people's wealth, and in return we give jobs to men in this field, men who automatically with the salary they receive and the money they spend help to create purchasing power which in turn is capable of helping private industry which has a responsibility to produce for the people.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, that is the best way to deal with unemployment. Each time those men are put to work on public projects, in a given sector, they get purchasing power which helps create more purchasing power-that is for workers in industry or the services-power to consume what industry can produce with a small percentage of workers.
Mr. Chairman, there is another thing we must ask ourselves about that measure. What interest will the municipalities have to pay?
If they are asked to pay a rather high rate of interest, say from 5 to 5| per cent, their yearly budget will again be burdened with another increase in debt charges. Now we find that today there are, in this country, a large number of municipalities, if not the majority of them, which have to spend 25, 30, 35 or even 45 per cent of their budgets on debt charges alone.
When that money is placed at their disposal through the Bank of Canada, the Bank of Canada will be able to lend it at administration cost, that is to say that the Bank of Canada will be able to lend money at one half per cent. At the same time, the municipalities will not have their budgets burdened with so much interest increasing their debts, for let us not forget that the more we give now to the municipalities, the more we help them service their debt which represents such a large portion of their budgets.
Then, what should the interest be? If the Minister of Finance is willing to seriously consider the motion for which he voted last year and to which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred earlier, that is the motion on debt free money and implement it, he will see to it that the Bank of Canada grant interest free loans to municipalities, that is loans without interest with the debt-free money from the Bank of Canada. Repayment then will be made much easier since the principal only and not principal plus interest will have to be repaid. We know that when a municipality has to

borrow an amount of $1,000 and to repay it with interest over 20 years it must pay twice the original amount of $1,000, thus paying twice for roads and buildings.
If the interest is low or if the loans are free from interest, the municipalities will pay the cost of construction only once.
So, Mr. Chairman, that is another important feature which should be included in this municipal development and loans legislation, namely interest free loans.
To illustrate how important interest can be to the municipalities, let us consider once again the matter of the Montreal subway. If the city of Montreal gets a loan of $200 million at an interest rate of 5 per cent to build the subway, every year, in interest alone, the municipality will have to pay $12 million to service its debt on the subway alone. If the amount is to be repaid over a period of 100 years, that is the life of the subway and the amount of depreciation alone-that is $200 million divided by 100 years-then, the municipality would be paying only $2 million a year and after a hundred years, the subway would be completely paid for, instead of paying $12 million a year on interest and after a hundred years not having even started payments on the capital borrowed and still owing the whole value of the subway which will be worn out by that time. That subway would then be completely useless and the municipality would have paid $12 million a year for it.
But in proceeding the way I suggested a while ago, the city of Montreal would be paying only $2 million a year and after a hundred years, the subway would be completely paid for.
Mr. Chairman, that is, in our opinion, a most important matter that the Minister of Finance will have to consider when he proposes the bill: an interest free loan and, most of all, a loan from the Bank of Canada. It is important to know where that money will come from. If it comes from the Bank of Canada, it will be new credit that will, more or less, increase the credit already in circulation and will make itself felt in the country as a whole as purchasing power that will enable Canadians to buy the equivalent of the increase in production.
A short while ago, I listened to the Leader of the Opposition talking about what he called "easy money". Mr. Chairman, we in this party call that adequate money to meet the needs of the country. It is not necessarily

Municipal Development and Loan Board easy money, it is not what is called easy money. It should be called adequate money, to achieve what is possible in our country.
It is possible to do that, since today, municipalities borrow largely on foreign markets; as a result foreign money is brought into our country and it is added to our own money supply. We would rather have our own Bank of Canada add money to the Canadian market.
The fact that money comes from one place or another-and I want the Minister of Finance to listen carefully

Mr. Chairman, a careful reading of the resolution that is now before us leads me to believe that the main purpose of this resolution is contained in the first line of it where it states that it is expedient to introduce a measure to promote increased employment in Canada. Now, far be it from me to criticize this government for any move it may make in this direction. However, it does seem odd to us that they would do so in this particular type of legislation.
What about the needs of the municipalities themselves? Should they not be the paramount consideration in any legislation dealing with municipalities? It would appear that the real needs of the municipalities are, in the main, ignored in this particular piece of legislation. Instead of this government going to the municipalities and saying, "You have some problems, can we help you with these problems?" the government seems to have said, "We have a problem that is of paramount importance and that problem is unemployment. We wonder if we can find some way in which we can get the municipalities to help with our problem?" There does not
[Mr. Gregoire.l
appear, Mr. Chairman, to be any recognition of the federal responsibility to our urban communities. There seems to be no acceptance of the changes that have taken place in our society.
At one time the most of the wealth in our society was in land and real estate, but that is no longer the case. Now, less and less of the wealth of the country is in these fields but they are still the main source of tax revenues for our municipalities across the country. In other words, our municipalities are like our farmers and many other groups in our society, they are caught in this sort of cost-price squeeze. The costs of the responsibilities of municipalities are going up inexorably year after year, but still the wealth which is the main source of tax revenues is to a lesser and lesser extent contained in real estate.
However, Mr. Chairman, before I give the wrong impression to the house I want to say that we in this party welcome this move, whatever the motive may have been. It appears to be a timid little step towards solving a most important need today, that is the need for adequate social capital. The members of this party have, for many years, expressed this need in this house. I do not intend to go into the details of that today. I should like, however, to try to draw attention to just how inadequate I believe this step is. When this resolution was first mentioned, there was a reference to a figure of $400 million. I distinctly got the impression that this would be the sum for a one year period. We were disappointed today to hear the minister say that this sum was to cover a three year rather than a one year period. This means that the amount to be made available in this field is about $125 million per year.
Just how adequate is this sum to meet the need? When we are going to test something like this, we should go to the best source available. I would suggest that one of the best sources available would be the present minister when he was acting in a different capacity. If we look at the final report of the commission on Canada's economic prospects, page 308, the section dealing with social requirements by municipalities 1956 to 1980, we find no less an authority than the minister saying that the need for social capital by municipalities over that period of time would amount to about $31,500 million. If calculated on a yearly basis, this sum would yield about $1,250 million per year. However, when the minister, acting in his present capacity, is finally in a position to do something about solving this problem we find he has cut this total sum to just about 10 per cent of what he felt the requirements

were at the time he made that assessment. It may be slightly over $125 million per year, but I am sure the comparison is a valid one.
Now, reverting once more to what appears to be the main purpose of this resolution, that is to provide additional employment, I may say we have to realize something else. We have to realize that this purpose can only be reached if this money is in excess of what is available through normal channels or is in excess of what is being done at the present time. If this money merely replaces capital that is being used in this field now, then we have solved nothing. It is true that the provision of this capital may be of some assistance to municipalities because it will give them necessary capital at a smaller rate of interest than they are paying at the present time. This will be true, certainly, if this provision for a 25 per cent forgiveness, or whatever term they have for it, goes into effect.
I noticed that during the minister's remarks he referred to the fact that this proposal would increase the capital available by about 50 per cent. I hope that as this debate progresses the minister will explain in more detail just how he arrived at this figure.
There is another matter too that we must take into consideration and I believe that some recognition of this has been given in the resolution by the use of the words "subject to the approval of the provinces concerned".
I think that is a very important matter to consider, especially when we find as we look across the country that many municipalities today are in the position of having borrowed right up to the maximum permitted by their provincial governments. Before the debate is finished I hope the minister will explain to the house and to the country just how municipalities in this position, and there are many of them, are going to derive any benefit from this legislation. However, as I say, there will be ample time and opportunity as debate on the resolution and the bill to follow proceeds to go into these details, so we shall await both the bill and the explanations of the minister with considerable interest.

He said: Mr. Speaker, since coming into the house this afternoon I have been given reason to believe that the government may refer this bill to the standing committee on veterans affairs. Because of the contemplated action by the government I shall cut my introductory remarks as short as possible. I first brought this bill before the house on March 13, 1962. I may have been very harsh in my words at that time and perhaps, because of the proposed action of the government today, I should temper them somewhat.
The purpose of the bill is set out in the explanatory notes where they say:
The purpose of this bill is to give an applicant for a pension under the Pension Act the right, where the pension commission or an appeal board has ruled against his or her entitlement, to have the decision reviewed by the courts-
-first on questions of law and second, on controversial issues of fact.
I understand there is a principle of Canadian law which states all members of the public have a right of access to the courts to determine their rights under the law. In this particular case the Pension Act is the law, but a veteran does not have that right under it. He cannot appeal to the courts. The present Pension Act denies that basic principle to a veteran, and denies him that right which all other citizens have.
When I first introduced this bill last year I stated:
The bill applies to the Pension Act that principle of the rule of law that, to the degree most possible, the decisions of an administrative tribunal or commission which touch the person, property or rights of an individual should be subject to review by the courts.
The United Kingdom has applied this rule of law to as many of its boards, tribunals and commissions as possible in the tribunals and inquiries act, 1958. The British parliament found it was necessary to protect the rights of the individual by guaranteeing an appeal to the courts from arbitrary tribunal decisions.

It is obvious that the intent of the Pension Act was to protect service personnel against the risks to which, by reason of their service, they were and are exposed. I do not believe the act should give the pension commission the right to substitute its views for the intent of parliament, but it has done that. I would like to read two sections of the Pension Act which, to me, take away the intent of parliament. First I refer to section 5(5) and this is what it says:
The commission shall determine any question of interpretation of this act and the decision of the commission on any such question is final.
In other words, it does not matter what parliament put into the act, it is how the commission interprets what we put into it that counts. I suggest here and now that if under section 70, the benefit of the doubt section, one of the controversial sections in the act, a veteran could appeal, not necessarily to the courts but to some commissioner or ombudsman, as he is called, I am quite sure he would have a just decision.
I also refer to section 65(3) which reads as follows:
Except as hereinafter otherwise provided, every decision of an appeal board of the commission is final.
That is quite definite and I say those two sections are contrary to one of the basic principles of Canadian law, namely that each subject should have the right of access to our courts to determine his rights. The right to appeal to our courts, by the veteran applicant, is taken away from him by section 5 and section 65(3).
Parliament in its wisdom, and at the request of the courts, enacted legislation known as the Interpretation Act, which should have been a guide to the pension commission and which is supposed to apply to all our laws with the exception of criminal laws. Section 15 of the Interpretation Act was inserted on the basis that the law as it existed perhaps did not do justice to some person or group of persons. Therefore parliament gives the person or persons affected a right, and a remedy, before the courts of the land.
By the inclusion of section 5 and section 65 in the Pension Act, veterans and veterans' dependants do not have the protection of anyone. They have not even got the protection of parliament at the present time. I believe the average individual citizen feels that he or she ought to be able to challenge, before some independent and impartial third party, any adverse decision made against him or her by a government official or a body of government officials, but this right is denied to our citizens donning any uniform of our armed services in the event that they 28902-5-58
Pension Act
have a pension claim. They are not guaranteed their rights against an arbitrary decision of the pension commission.
We must admit the Pension Act as it is now on our statute books is law, but many of us do not believe it is just law. Law and justice are not the same thing. I would suggest the Pension Act, as it now reads, is not good legislation and I do not believe it intended to give so much power to a tribunal as it apparently has given to it. A review of parliament's intention can be determined by reading the debates in Hansard when the Pension Act was passed and subsequently amended from time to time. However the real test of any legislation is in its administration, and this to me is where this act particularly appears to be discriminatory. I am informed by the pension commission that when it makes its decisions it is governed by precedent. Some of us may think it should be governed by common sense. A review of some of the decisions handed down by the board will bring to light the ridiculous use of the word "precedent" by the pension commission. There is no consistency in the reasons for the decisions handed down by the board, and what they call precedent has no rhyme or reason. To illustrate my contention that there is no precedent governing the decisions of the board and that their findings are discriminatory, I would ask the house to compare a few reasons or decisions handed down by the board in order to see how narrow and small are some of them. I would refer hon. members to a case to which I referred in March of last year, when I said this:
I would refer hon. members to the evidence of the vice chairman of the Canadian pension commission, as recorded on May 18, 1961 in the minutes of proceedings on veterans affairs. Referring to one case, the reason for the decision was as follows:
"He went across the street and delivered the message, stepped out of the door and was hit by a truck. If he had been hit going in the door, before he had delivered the message, he would have been pensionable; however, he was hit when he went out the door, and he was not pensionable."
More liberal decisions have been made, I admit, by the pension board when the service personnel concerned were not even on duty. I would refer the house to one other case as an example. This was in regard to an R.C.A.F. man killed while flying for a civilian flying club. I will not reveal the name but I would just refer to this case. This is the decision handed down and the reason for granting a pension:
This board, after a comprehensive study of all the circumstances attendant upon this case, concluded that the applicant, although not on duty at the time of the fatal accident was by his efforts making a contribution in the best interests of the Royal Canadian Air Force. Service compulsion does not appear to be involved in this case, but the interests of the service would appear to be so.

Pension Act
Invoking to the full the provisions of section 70, it is therefore concluded that the accident causing death was directly connected with regular force service in peacetime.
I would point out that another contentious passage in the Pension Act, as many veterans know, is section 13(2). The last line of that section reads-
-arose out of or was directly connected with such military service.
It does not seem to be very difficult for most of us to connect an accident with either of those provisions, but I would ask hon. members to try putting a case before the pension commission and see how far they get with this section or section 5(5), because the interpretation of the act is entirely a matter for the board. We have cases where a pension has been given to a serviceman on leave, and I have one such case here:
The man was on leave just prior to discharge. He was ordered to report to Ottawa for discharge. Returning from leave to report, he crashed into a standing bus, suffering chest injuries which resulted in permanent disability.
He was given a pension. I would also suggest that when an applicant engages the services of a prominent lawyer his chances of a favourable decision are greatly increased. The appearance of a prominent, qualified lawyer seems to influence what I maintain is an unqualified board, in the realm of interpreting the law. I have another case here which I imagine deals with a sailor who was on leave at the time. I am not going to read all the facts, but he had a gunshot wound in the back as a result of being in the path of a robbery. This is the decision handed down by the board:
The facts of the case are not in dispute, the only issue being, did the incident arise out of or was it directly connected with peacetime service. The undersigned were impressed-
I would ask the house to listen to this passage. The "undersigned" were the board:
The undersigned were impressed with the learned counsel's argument and conclude that whereas the sequence of events leading up to the injurious accident cannot be classified as entirely peculiar to military service-
And so on.
However, they did grant him a pension under section 70. I do not deny the fact that in the last three cases to which I made reference these people were entitled to a pension, but the decisions and results are very difficult to relate to the first case that I mentioned, where the chap went in the door and delivered the message, came out of the door and was hit, and the pension board decided that if he had been hit going in, he would have been pensionable, but as he was hit coming out, he was not pensionable. How does one explain that to an applicant?

To me and to the dependants in this case it would seem there is strong evidence for the charge of discrimination. I am reminded of a recent editorial which appeared in one of our local newspapers commenting on the Gordon Knott case, which was debated in this house not too long ago. I am not going to read the whole editorial, but shall read part of it. The article is headed "There should be a right of appeal" and states:
It is when action is taken in secret, and without the chance of appeal for the redress of grievances, that the possibility of mistake, injustice and arbitrariness may become serious.
Later on the article says:
It would seem desirable that some method of appeal against arbitrary action should be found-
That is what I am suggesting in connection with the Pension Act. If the house will not pass this bill or the government will not take steps-although I hope that they will take steps-to amend the present act, I hope they will give consideration at this time to appointing what is commonly known as a special parliamentary commissioner, or, as I said previously, an ombudsman, a person who could investigate these complaints and bring them to the attention of those on the treasury benches or some supreme authority which would act on them.
I intended, Mr. Speaker, to say something about section 13(2). I also wanted to tell the house about the support I have received for this bill from many Legion branches across Canada. I would also say that if this bill were accepted, the pension commission could itself appeal to the courts regarding the interpretation of the law. However, as I have asked hon. members to desist from talking too long perhaps I had better sit down myself. I wish to thank the government for the consideration I hope they will give to this bill by referring it to the veterans affairs committee, at which time I will have more to say.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPEAL TO COURTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the introduction of this small but not unimportant bill. At the same time I can assure the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) that I shall compress my remarks into a narrow compass. As I understand the bill-if I may make a few general observations-its underlying principle is to maintain public confidence in our tribunals and commissions by making sure that under proper circumstances there is a right of appeal to our courts of law. There is a growing concern among the public that as our life has become more complicated, we are subjected more and more to the restrictions of commissions and tribunals; that there is an encroachment upon private right and private interest. This danger

was exposed as long ago as 1929 by Lord Hewart in his book "The New Despotism". I do not suggest for one moment that the introduction of tribunals and commissions ipso facto leads to a restriction of private rights; on the contrary, many commissions have extended private rights. However, the danger of the collision between the private right and the public interest is always there and in this somewhat uneven fight I respectfully suggest that it is essential that in proper circumstances there should be a right of appeal to our courts of law.
This bill contains, in my respectful opinion, the seeds of three good principles. In the first place, it would mean that an unsuccessful applicant would at least be assured that he has had a full and careful consideration of his appeal. If this recourse is denied to him, as it is now, it means he has been judged by a commission consisting of appointees of the minister. The danger of this situation is that an applicant may feel he has come up against a blank wall of unfettered ministerial discretion. If he were granted the right of appeal and, again, this would only be by leave, he would have the feeling that careful and unbiased consideration had been given to his petition.
The next point I wish to raise is this: without casting any reflection whatsoever on the present commission which has, I believe, done outstanding work and provided a speedy way of exercising the rights of individuals, I believe it is fundamentally true that whatever tribunal or court is rendering a decision, if it is aware that there is another court above it to pass on what it is doing, it automatically gives more careful and anxious consideration to the matters before it.
The third point I wish to make is this: I feel it is imperative that the work of all commissions and tribunals should from time to time be reviewed by our courts. I realize that when an application is successfully made for leave to appeal, the court of appeal would be dealing only with one individual case. But such a situation often leads to the entire mechanism of the tribunal or commission concerned being brought before the scrutiny of the appeal court. These things are fundamental to the proper working of a democracy.
I am somewhat concerned about the proposed section 68A which grants both to the individual and to the commission the right to apply for leave to appeal. Looking at section 68A(1) (c) it appears that this would cover a case where the commission would be appealing an award to an individual on the ground that it had been obtained by fraud or misrepresentation. As I understand the proposed amendment it would appear that 28902-5-58i
Pension Act
application for leave to appeal in these circumstances would be an ex parte motion. In other words, the individual concerned would not be present at the application. I respectfully suggest that when the commission is taking steps to withdraw a pension from an individual that person should be entitled to be heard and to make representations at the moment when application is made for leave to appeal. This is a matter which concerns me seriously and I suggest that the procedure in connection with leave to appeal should be spelled out in detail in the bill.
With these words, I shall conclude. As I say, I welcome the bill and I trust it will be dealt with expeditiously.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to contribute a few comments on this bill I wish to say I admire its sponsor, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) and the way the bill was presented so forcefully in the last parliament. I refer to the hon. member's address delivered on March 13, 1962. He has indicated his belief that the bill now before us is the solution to this problem, just as he did when the government of which he was a supporter was in power. He put the measure forward forcefully and well. A number of us have had an opportunity to examine the reactions to the bold presentation he made at that time.
I do not think there is much dispute about the fact that there have been decisions which we find hard to accept and hard to understand. The hon. member indicated how ridiculous it was that a decision could give one result when a man went across the street to deliver a message, and another should he be hit while he was leaving the door. This is not the only case of this sort. There have been a number of cases where the pension commission has reached conclusions which we find hard to accept. But there is another problem here, one which I think we must consider without doing violence to any of the sentiments uttered by the hon. member. I think he is presenting the case from the viewpoint of the lawyer. This is almost the kind of presentation one might expect to receive from the Canadian Bar Association. Characteristically lawyers tend to think that the best solution lies by the process of appeal. It is easy for me to understand that point of view.
As parliamentarians, however, we have sometimes to divorce our thoughts from our vocations and recognize that as government has developed and as legislation has become more complex over the years, a large number of administrative tribunals and bodies having judicial or quasi-judicial powers have come into being. I think it could fairly be maintained by a student of political economy that the bill now before us, an attempt to amend the Pension Act by providing for judicial appeal, is in principle retrograde. It represents an attack on the whole modern concept of administrative law, which indicates that there are certain problems sufficiently specialized as to call for detailed technical evidence. In this case, the case of pensions, we are largely concerned with medical cases. Often times there is need of speedy decision. We are faced with the likelihood of claimants frequently being without 
resources and unable to support the lengthy and costly process of appeal. Also, these pension decisions deal with questions of fact as well as with law, and in a manner sometimes very difficult to distinguish. It is this combination of facts and law which sometimes renders an administrative tribunal precisely the right kind of place to hear this peculiar type of claim.
I am sure that many of us in this house have had cases where we have taken issue with the workmen's compensation board. In my own case I have in mind the board in Ontario. Yet if we look at the literature on the subject throughout the world we find that our workmen's compensation act has been cited as a model. It would appear to students of this legislation who have studied it in depth that the act provides solutions and quick justice for people, a situation which, I say regrettably, cannot always be obtained through our normal processes of litigation. It is suggested that an appeal to the courts or some of these tribunals would be retrograde in the sense of being time-consuming, and one can suggest to this house how timeconsuming it might be if we had to appeal to the court of appeal of a province or to the Supreme Court of Canada. It becomes, of necessity, a process which is costly, and in all likelihood cumbersome. We all know that courts often tend to be overloaded, which might very easily lead to further delays. The way in which our courts dispose of their business illustrates a great inequity in work loads in different courts in different parts of Canada.
Then, judges do not always have that intimate knowledge and understanding of the type of case which presumably would come before the pension commission. We might have a situation where the court of appeal of a province makes a wise and sensible decision, and yet another court of appeal in another province which might have had virtually no experience in this type of legislation on the same facts might come to a very poor decision. I do not know what the answer to this is. As I say, the approach of lawyers, individually and collectively and certainly of the Canadian Bar Association would be that we should always have appeals. I think there would be large support for the submission of the hon. member that decisions should be reviewed, and that there should be a tribunal or some other body which can re-examine the case. Yet in the matter of pensions I think experience has tended to prove that certain classes of pensioners have been very fairly treated indeed. I think it is the consensus among veterans that servicemen of world war I and world war II are getting a good hearing

before the pension commission. That is because of the insurance principle. It has been said that all a man has to establish to become pensionable is that he was there.
It seems to me, from what I can judge and inquiries I have been able to make, that the complaints lie largely with the type of case referred to by the hon. member, that of the permanent force soldier, sailor or airman who is not accorded this same protection, and who must establish that his injury arose out of, or was directly connected with, military service. The hon. member has referred the house to section 13(2) of the Pension Act. At the moment the pension board consists of 13 members three of whom are lawyers. In my opinion there are not enough lawyers. Perhaps we have too many lawyers in some places, but I believe there are not enough on the pension commission. It is precisely the kind of case referred to by the hon. member which, I think, has thrown confusion into the decisions of the pension board.
I was particularly concerned about the case of a nursing sister, a sublieutenant in the Royal Canadian Navy, who came before the appeal board in December 1959 with regard to the accidental fracture of her right tibia and fibula, and who received an adverse decision. She was serving at H.M.C.S. Cornwallis, as a hospital operation room nurse and was the only nurse detailed. She was required to stay in the north block and eat in the wardroom, and had to be on the station. This nursing sister was subject to emergency calls at any time. She drove her car, which she had tacit authority to use, from the barracks to the wardroom before reporting to the hospital for normal duty. She parked her car, went towards the wardroom and slipped on a very icy, unsanded surface. This attractive young lady with a fine career before her suffered very serious injury. One of the most powerful and influential members of this house at that time, the hon. member who represented Dufferin-Simcoe in the last house, and who certainly, it would be supposed, would have had the ear of the government, exercised himself on her behalf to see that her case was fairly and well put before the commission. I know this was done, because of the interest of this hon. gentleman of unusual parliamentary experience and ability. Yet the pension commission came to the decision that the incident did not arise from military service. The fact that she had to have her breakfast before reporting to the hospital and had slipped on a very icy surface at H.M.C.S. Cornwallis apparently did not commend itself to the members of this commission, who I think were laymen. They decided that the injury did not arise out of her military service.
Pension Act
Mr. Speaker, what is the solution? I think the solution has been suggested by the hon. member who presented his case so well today. He spoke of the possibility of a parliamentary commissioner, or ombudsman; or, if I may refer to a bill I have on the order paper, a people's tribune. But surely there should be, not only for this kind of case but for a whole variety of cases resulting from decisions arrived at by administrative tribunals, some recourse in extraordinary cases where a claimant could put his particular set of facts before such an officer and as a result perhaps have a new opportunity to present his case.
In my opinion, just as in the sad case to which my hon. friend from Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) referred, I think the Chambers case should be named where a young serviceman died on November 18, 1957, and the appeal board hearing took place on May 12, 1959. It does not seem right that that tragic result should occur without some kind of solution or remedy being provided for the dependants. Surely we are not satisfied with this kind of conclusion. Yet, Mr. Speaker, over the past few years we have had as the best advocate, I submit, for servicemen both of world war I and world war II, and also for members of the permanent force, the Royal Canadian Legion. Certainly we must pay close attention to the Legion when they address themselves to problems relating to pensions. This is something they know a great deal about.
I should like to refer the house to The Legionary of July 1960, which contains a report of the resolutions committee of that year. On page 15 of the report there is a heading entitled "Explanation of Appeal Provisions", and the text reads as follows:
At the Edmonton convention it was resolved that the dominion executive council bring in a report for the next dominion convention on the desirability of establishing an appeal from the pension commission to an independent authority. This resolution was referred to the members of the veterans welfare advisory committee, who made an extensive study of the problem and considered the opinions of a large number of people with first-hand knowledge of the circumstances and background of the whole matter. This committee reported to council through its chairman, comrade Mervyn Woods, to the following effect:
1.	The present legislation and procedure is basically sound and the establishment of an appeal board would not serve to advance the interests of the veteran.
2.	There are a number of ways in which the commission may improve its operations and bring them in line with the intent and purpose of the statute under which it is established. These include:
(a) Use of section 8 to make regulations in respect of procedure to be followed instead of allowing unwritten policies to have the effect of regulations without the knowledge of those to whom they apply.

Pension Act
Then, paragraph (b) refers to the proper use of the benefit of doubt clause. I shall not read any further, but hon. members who are interested in this submission could refer to The Legionary and consider the report of this resolutions committee of the Royal Canadian Legion.
I am not satisfied that any committee is always wise. I am sure that the hon. member has brought forward a very important point. There are cases in which the decisions are clearly unjust, unreasonable and not sensible at all. In so far as the two cases to which reference has been made are concerned, I do not believe these were fair conclusions, having in mind the kind of conclusion that lawyers would have expected to arrive at before a civil court under similar circumstances. I believe that if either of these cases had come before a civil court and had been heard on appeal, there would have been a different kind of decision.
From what little I have been able to determine in connection with some of these cases- and as outsiders we cannot discover too many details-I believe there have been cases in which the commission has been confused between its duty on the one hand to the applicant and, on the other hand, the need to protect the public purse.
There is another problem, and it seems to me that this is inherent in the report that was handed down by this resolutions committee as reported in The Legionary of July, 1960. I am told that years ago there was an appeal process. I am told that soldiers and some experienced veterans who have been doing work for veterans groups over the years came to distrust the appeal procedure. Their experience has indicated that, on balance, the appeal procedure did not work too well for the veteran. After all, if the applicant for a pension can appeal, it seems only proper that the crown likewise can appeal. I believe that most of us feel that, in many cases, the pension commission have winked their eyes a little at factors that might not have been too helpful to the applicant in order that the commission might render an equitable and generous verdict. The fact that we are private members of parliament places us in a position where we are addressing ourselves frequently to this kind of problem. We understand the problems of our constituents, and applicants who have a very reasonable case to put before the government. On the other hand, we know that the public purse has to be protected against unfair claims.
I feel, therefore, that the solution is not to be found in this particular bill. We respect the hon. member who introduced the measure. We know that he has been a champion
[Mr. Matheson.l
of the veteran. He has this reputation not only in his own province but across the country. He has done the veterans a service in throwing light on the inequity of some decisions handed out to some applicants. It seems to me the solution to the problem lies in some other remedy than the one provided in the hon. member's bill.
If one looks over the private members' bills presented to this house, he finds that basically there are two things about which members are thinking. There seems to have been a great deal of concern about consumer credit, and the second most important thing, if I read these bills correctly, is the need for some kind of adequate protection against the inequities if not injustices that result from decisions of administrative tribunals. Sometimes the members of these tribunals are trying to follow the legislation as fairly as they can. They cannot help it if the result appears to be unfair.
It is clear that, in so far as the cases referred to are concerned, the commission tried to follow the precise wording of the legislation. I hope the answer to this problem may be found during the twenty sixth parliament in which no party is in a position of dominance. Perhaps by working together we can come up with a solution by providing for a people's tribune, ombudsman or something of the sort, and thus allow some kind of reconsideration of these decisions.

We know that the hon. gentleman is introducing his bill with the idea of doing something to correct a certain situation he considers exists under the present law.
However, let me say this: While we are sympathetic to his purpose I think we should tread cautiously in respect of this type of legislation. The previous speaker mentioned the workmen's compensation act. I am sure he will be interested to know that British Columbia was the first province in Canada to have

a workmen's compensation act because the labour organizations in that province pressed for that very strongly from the early days of this century. However, those who have been interested in the administration of the workmen's compensation act in British Columbia, and in other provinces, have also been interested in proposals made from time to time for the right of appeal to the courts against decisions of compensation boards. Invariably, after consideration by various labour organizations and other persons interested in the best procedure to provide the best results, they have come to the conclusion that they were safer to leave their cases in the hands of the workmen's compensation boards. In many instances, the companies have much more money than the workers or the trade unions. This has been the experience of those interested in this type of legislation under compensation boards which have to do with civilian casualties, just as this legislation has to do with the casualties of war.
Now, this matter has been discussed by the various branches of the Royal Canadian Legion and other veterans' organizations. I understand that the matter was discussed at the last convention, but to date the Legion has not taken any position on this question. I think it is fair to say that they are interested in all proposals. I do not think it is necessary to take the time to go into the arguments for and against this bill, particularly since I heard the hon. member who introduced the bill mention the fact that the government was quite willing to have it referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs. I think the subject matter of the bill should be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs where we can have witnesses called before the committee, where we can get the opinions of the representatives of the veterans through the Royal Canadian Legion and through other veterans organizations, and hear the pros and cons as the result of weighing the evidence and as the result of experience. I suggest that would be the best way to deal with this quite important question at this time. After hearing evidence the committee could then come to conclusions and make a report to the house on this very interesting bill. With these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I conclude.

Mr. Speaker, in so far as the bill is concerned my observations will be brief. In principle it is highly acceptable. I should like to underline the very true observation made by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) when he stated that law and justice are not similar. Permit me to continue in French.
