speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that burst of applause from a packed house gives one a great deal of confidence and desire to continue this debate. At five o'clock, when I was saved by the bell, I was expressing concern about the fact that the large metropolitan areas would gain most from the proposed legislation that we are considering by way of this preliminary resolution. Yet, I think it is correct to say unemployment is highest in the less settled areas.
I think it is right to say the minister this afternoon suggested the priority which the government has given to the introduction of this resolution showed it to be one of the most important decisions of the much heralded program for action; but is it not interesting that this veritable keystone in the attack on unemployment should take the form of new borrowings by the municipalities? This is a fact, no matter what the forgiveness provisions, write-offs or other lures may be. I suppose we have to admit that almost every new program devised by government has the effect of increasing taxes, but I suggest the scheme proposed by this resolution is more cleverly indirect and obscure than most. Perhaps this is symbolic of our age, that the public can be so easily seduced by high-sounding policy statements.

Obviously all responsible members of parliament have a duty to consider carefully any measure that has as its objective increased employment, and a fair debate on any measure to increase employment would have to cover those helpful plans of the former government. I am not going to fall victim to my own advice by listing the achievements of another government, but there is one I want to mention as an example of what I call the creative use of money.
The shipbuilding subsidy program has meant a great deal to my constituency, and I might mention my constituency is what the textbooks of the twentieth century call the bedroom of the urban areas. It is where the workers who labour in the cities live. When I mention that program I am thinking of the Saint John Shipbuilding & Drydock Company which, within a period of a few years, has advanced from a couple of hundred employees-just a skeleton staff-with old worn-down equipment, to a firm employing about 2,800 people. This is largely, but not entirely, due to the shipbuilding subsidy program, and is also due to the initiative and drive of the present chairman of the board.
This program appeals to me because it uses federal moneys creatively. I only hope that on Thursday the Minister of Finance will catalogue other programs of this creative type, and this leads me to the hope and expectation that the capital projects approved by the board contemplated in this resolution will fall largely into what might be called creative social capital schemes. The only trouble is that when we start talking about social capital my hon. friends to my left, in a literal but not in any other sense, place upon the expression other meanings. They include wonderful testimonials with coloured water, which enlightened Canadians via television during the last election campaign.
As I mentioned at five oclock, Mr. Chairman, this is not new legislation. In 1938 parliament passed an act to assist municipalities in making self-liquidating loans. I am not going to go over that ground; but parliament was then, as it must be now, concerned about the constitutional aspect of the legislation, and the interesting thing in 1938 was that the device used provided that the provinces should guarantee all loans approved. This was an interesting device to avoid a constitutional problem, because surely it was redundant to have the provinces guarantee loans already granted by the federal government?	.
I am also interested in the formula which the proposed board will use in approving loans. Will it be the same as in 1938 on a per capita basis to the amount of the loan? That is, will the aggregate amount of loans

to a municipality be proportionate to the $400 million which the population of that municipality might bear to the population of Canada? There will be some interesting juggling and pressuring, if pressuring is a word we are entitled to use in parliament. If there is not some fair and equitable system of sharing, then the fund will be quickly gobbled up by the large metropolitan areas.
Recently I was reading the catalogue of projects the municipalities have already proposed. I think they are up to $180 million. We are only at the resolution stage of the bill and we have not yet heard from Her Worship, the Mayor of Ottawa. May I again remind the house-and this is the danger I find myself in as a representative of one of the extremes of Canada, not a political extreme but an extreme of unemployment- that this legislation is designed to help the larger cities of Canada, and it will not really touch the grave problem of regional unemployment. Smaller cities and towns will not benefit because of the restrictions placed on the projects. Sewerage, hospitals, and slum clearance projects are all excluded because they are covered by other legislation, and presumably expressways, roads, streets and sidewalks will be the basic items of interest to all but the larger municipal areas.
Just because the house is slowly filling up I wish to give it the benefit of my own white paper. I have issued a white paper and have been assisted in this by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. I have done this because I do not think any consideration of a resolution such as this would be complete without a white paper. I have two tables; I am not going to file them but I shall read them.

Even in 1955 the outstanding net debt of the municipalities was $2,328.4 million and that year there was an increase of $259.9 million, well over half the amount that this generous government is adding to the funding of municipalities. Then, because the Secretary of State has expressed interest in having both tables, I am going to give him table B, which is the municipal direct and guaranteed bonds. This is interesting because you have the gross new issues delivered in each year, and then you take the retirements from that and get the net new issues, in case anybody doubts me. This summary is taken from the February, 1963 supplement to the Bank of Canada statistical summary. I am trying to indicate, of course, that the $400 million is going to be used up before the Secretary of State has had time to blow his nose; or is it sneezing that is the new device the present government uses to explain our problems?
In its submission to the royal commission on banking and finance last October the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities referred to forecasts made. I am sure they are accurate because they were made in 1957 by the Gordon commission. Emphasizing that no provision was made for mass transit and commuter railway facilities, nor was there any apparent inclusion for the municipal costs of urban redevelopment, the federation brief continued with these words:
Despite these omissions-
And they are basic:
-the commission estimated that by 1980 social capital expenditures will be required in Canada to the amount of $19.5 billion for roads and streets; $4.2 billion for school and universities; $2.7 billion for hospitals; $2.7 billion for sewerage systems; and $2.4 billion for waterworks.

Municipal Development and Loan Board
The total estimate of capital expenditures on these items alone amounts to $31.5 billion. The greater part of these expenditures will devolve upon municipal governments.
If there is validity in these estimated figures-and, with great respect, I suggest there is because they were made by so distinguished a person-then by 1980 the aggregate municipal debt of Canada for these purposes will have soared from its present approximate $4 billion to a figure somewhere in the range of $20 billion to $25 billion. Even if it is only half this figure it will be a staggering amount; in fact, so staggering that any further consideration of it on my humble part would be superfluous.
May I say that I hope the minister will assure us that emphasis and priority will be placed on loans to areas with high unemployment. This to my mind is the only formula that would be proper, the only formula that would fulfil the much heralded Liberal promise and the only formula which would in any way do what the resolution says it will do, that is try to meet the unemployment problem. If this is the yardstick the minister proposes-that is, the yardstick of area and regional help to try to solve unemployment- and if the capital funds are not swallowed up entirely by the great metropolises of Canada, then I suggest the legislation will be beneficial to Canadians. But without that assurance I will have to reserve judgment as to how I will vote on the resolution and the bill.

Mr. Chairman, first of all, as this is the first time I have the opportunity of addressing you since you have occupied the position of chairman, I hope you will bear me no grudge if, as a former colleague at the University of Ottawa, I express all the satisfaction your appointment gave me, as well as your many friends.
I wish you great success in the discharge of your responsibilities, which you are already doing with so much distinction and competence.
I would also like to take this opportunity to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), who introduced the resolution, a few questions. He tried to justify its usefulness by stating that this was a remedy, and one of the main remedies, which the government had to offer to reduce unemployment, i.e. a palliative against unemployment, but I wonder if the end actually justifies the means.
Does not the project basically encroach upon provincial jurisdiction, even if the provinces give their nominal agreement? With regard to this matter, what guarantees does the minister give us? None, so to speak, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) does not
[Mr. Fairweather.J

give any either, if we consider the very weak answer he gave the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), this afternoon, when he suggested that he would convene a federal-provincial conference on the matter. Now, Mr. Chairman, we do not even know if there has been any consultation with the provinces in this respect.
Have there been any discussions on this matter? Has there been any exchange of correspondence between the central government, that is the Minister of Finance, or some of his colleagues, or even the Prime Minister, and the heads of provincial governments?
Does the minister really intend to table in the house the correspondence putting forward views on the project which is now before the committee? And if there has been consultation, did it have any bearing on amendments to be made to the municipal code, in other words, the cities and towns act of the province of Quebec, to enable the municipalities, which I trust everybody in this house will agree, are subservient to the provinces, owe their existence to the provincial government which created them in such a way that, in any respect, they come under provincial jurisdiction.
For instance, was any consideration given to the borrowing capacity of municipalities, because unless I am mistaken, there are in the municipal code provisions on the borrowing power of municipalities and if we changed those today, we would adopt an act which would unilaterally modify the borrowing capacity of municipal governments.
This, in my opinion, is an important aspect of this legislation.
Was the additional burden for the municipalities considered, a burden the municipalities will have to face as they will have to repay both principal and interests on municipal loans, and this will also affect the taxpayers?
Perhaps the minister is prepared to go along with debt free money, which he recommended here not so long ago, I would even say with some vigour, in this house, but this afternoon he observed a cautious silence on that point.
However, we are entitled to a frank and clear statement from the hon. minister on this matter, so that we may know whether or not he is actually in favour of debt free money. Well, that is his business, the government's business, but he should at least have the courage to tell the house or the committee, in order that hon. members may be fully informed on this resolution and cast their votes accordingly.

I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if Mr. Lesage, the premier of the province of Quebec, has been consulted in this matter, and if so, what was his answer? Did he, for instance, give the Prime Minister of Canada the same answer as he gave on April 4 to the leader of the opposition, in the Quebec legislature?
That is what Mr. Lesage said on that occasion, as reported in Le Devoir of April 5 last. I shall quote his words to the committee, in order to clear up this argument which I am referring to. Mr. Johnson asked Mr. Lesage what he thought of the speech made the day before, in Montreal, by the present head of the government, the Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, who was trying at that time, to get votes as leader of the opposition, and to carry favour with the Quebec voters. Mr. Pearson had mentioned federal aid, with regard to sewers and water mains for the municipalities. And Mr. Lesage answered-I want to call the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to this answer, because I consider it very revealing-as follows:
I do not know in the slightest-
So he stated-
-what Mr. Pearson may have said about sewers and water mains, and I do not care-
Those are strong words.
-and I do not care whatever he may have said. The important thing is not what he may have said on this matter or another, but that we, here, are forming a strictly autonomist government-
That is what my hon. fellow members opposite should keep in mind.
Whatever the result of the elections on April 8 will be, we shall continue to support and uphold the rights of the province of Quebec, as the minister of municipal affairs did so well.
That is what Mr. Lesage said.
He was speaking, at that time, of Mr. Laporte, provincial minister of municipal affairs.
Mr. Laporte had, indeed, been most categorical in pointing out the danger of federal encroachment on municipal affairs when addressing the Montreal chamber of commerce. He was not the only one to do so. Most of our hon. friends opposite, who are now sitting on the government benches, have done so on various occasions.
Indeed, I defy any one of them, whoever he be, to tell this committee that their attitude had been different. I remember, for instance, some words spoken by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier), when he was sitting on this side of the house, on October 29, 1962, and I quote:
Municipal Development and Loan Board During the whole election campaign, we tried to show the Canadian people how the municipal loan fund, if applied in the province of Quebec, would encroach upon its autonomy, as in all other provinces.
But the minister sticks to generalities and goes no further. He offers no explanation on how a Liberal government would proceed to comply with the autonomy of the provinces in that matter.
The Minister without Portfolio and the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. La-montagne), author of an intriguing book on Canadian federalism, seemed at one time to have a well-timed repentance for his centralizing tendencies.
I remember in particular reading a report on a convention held in Quebec where he was chosen candidate for the Quebec East riding. At that time, exactly like his leader who had come to support his nomination, he frankly and clearly stated he was in favour of a withdrawal from joint programs.
Mr. Chairman, not only is there no question of withdrawing from those programs, but we are going further in that direction. I therefore ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. La-montagne), the Minister of Justice and others to explain to members of this committee how you can withdraw from an over-all plan and, at the same time, go further in the same direction. After all, I think one must be consistent.
What is exactly the constitutional position? It is a well-known fact that in the past, the Liberal party, when in power, during that famous period of 22 years, interfered in various ways and with much impertinence in the provincial field, including the one concerning municipal activities and functions. Indeed, a recital of those facts would be tedious, Mr. Chairman.
However, section 92 of the constitution is quite clear and does provide for the rights of provincial states; it provides particularly that municipal institutions come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. How could it be otherwise, when municipalities exist only through the provincial state which created them? That is an elementary principle which no one will oppose. Well, the government, in this legislation and in some other which was put on the order paper, now interferes in that field by proposing expenses to settle municipal problems. I am not even sure that this is a solution to municipal problems, but the interference is not less clear nor less flagrant. Last April, a few days before the election, the Minister without Portfolio was delivering an address to the students of the University of
912	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board Montreal, protesting that he was not a centralizer. He even denied the tendencies expressed in his book on federalism published in 1954.
Unfortunately, like many others, he is learning at his own expense that one must always weigh one's words. He should probably have become a notary. However, inadvertently or through lack of logic and while asserting his deep conviction as an autonomist, eager to respect provincial jurisdiction in all fields, and particularly in the municipal field, the Minister without Portfolio who was then candidate for the riding of Outremont-St. Jean, stated that he was in favour of granting loans to municipalities. Moreover, as everyone knows, that proposal was included in the platform of the Liberal party as published and disseminated in the recent electoral campaign.
But what do they mean when they say: "We will secure the agreement of the provinces"? To me, it means that the government realizes that it impinges through joint programs upon a field which lies outside its jurisdiction. As a matter of fact, it might be appropriate to mention what Mr. Laporte, the Quebec municipal affairs minister, stated on this matter. I quote:
If the federal government, whichever party is in power, has money to spend for examination and solution of municipal problems, that money should rightly belong to the provincial authorities because they are the only ones to have any authority to deal with those problems.
Before he was elected a member, the hon. Minister without Portfolio said that his government would endeavour to implement legislative and fiscal decentralization, but now the government he belongs to goes back on those fine words and, which is worse, violates and even mocks a basic principle, under the cover of economic necessity, thus infringing upon provincial autonomy.
Mr. Laporte previously stated that his government would resist such an infringement and would insist on giving directly to the municipalities the amounts it wants them to have. This is undoubtedly the meaning of the ultimatum served by the premier of Quebec to the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, I do not understand too well why this government, by interfering further in a matter of purely provincial jurisdiction, chooses to ignore that ultimatum, and I wish that the Minister of Finance, who moved this resolution, would give us some


positive reasons for that because we must know the facts if we want to pass judgment knowingly. Up to now, neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Finance, nor any other member of the cabinet has even attempted to explain what means would be used to maintain provincial autonomy in the field of municipal affairs.
Mr. Chairman, maybe I have dwelt a bit too long on this problem but I consider it a basic issue and I believe that at the very beginning of this new regime, the new administration must prove that they have principles, not only to make a show of them during the election campaign, but to implement them in the legislation they will submit to this house.
Mr. Chairman, in the light of the constitution, the laws of the province of Quebec, the civil and the municipal codes, in a word, all the provincial statutes, I submit that we are witnessing a glaring violation of provincial jurisdiction. That is why I say that this government will have to supply much more information than the vague assurance it has given us up to now to justify its draft measure. And such information must be given not only to the house, but primarily-and that is most important-to the people of this country and more particularly to the people of the province of Quebec which I am sure from the statements I just quoted do not intend to give away the minutest part of their rights in this field or in any other, which belongs to them.
Therefore, until the Minister of Finance or another government spokesman gives us that information and until we receive satisfactory answers, that proposal will only be, in my opinion, a Trojan horse, in short, a proposal that will have to be studied with care and mistrust.
I am sure that the motive that inspired this measure is commendable in so far as it brings a solution to unemployment. But why not give the provinces the money needed so that they can carry out those projects themselves? In so doing, we would respect not only the letter but also the spirit of the constitution.
So far, the Minister of Finance has told us that he intends to stay within the constitution, to respect the letter and spirit of it, but he has failed to convince us in that respect.

Mr. Chairman, I have no hesitation in saying that when we saw this resolution on the order paper and listened to some of its aims and objectives we in this party thought we had at least some proposed

legislation which was going to do something about the tremendous rise in capital costs to the municipalities, about which my hon. friend from Royal spoke a few moments ago. As a matter of fact, I have some press clippings before me following the Prime Minister's speech to the federation of mayors and municipalities. I have a headline in the Toronto Daily Star which says: "$400 million is ready in loans to make jobs-Prime Minister". I have another in the Ottawa Journal lor May 30 which says: "Come and get it, P.M. urges the mayors". The Globe and Mail has this headline: "Municipal lending terms will be generous-Mr. Pearson".
So, Mr. Chairman, we thought that this was going to be designed to help the municipal governments all over Canada with their problems of capital costs and so on. I have a press clipping from the Toronto Daily Star which says, in effect, that the Prime Minister's proposal to introduce a bill to set up a municipal development and loan fund was greeted by applause from the delegates to the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. Well, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that if those same delegates had been here this afternoon when the Minister of Finance outlined some of the conditions that were to be attached to the granting of these loans, they may not have applauded quite so loudly.
The minister began the introduction of this resolution by pointing out some of the aims and objectives of the legislation being introduced. Certainly, no hon. member from any corner of this house would disagree with some of those aims. He mentioned that the government was aware of the unemployment problem, and suggested that the municipalities could, in fact, stimulate employment more rapidly than any other level of government. I have no disagreement with this statement. I think it is true. He also claimed that this legislation would initiate action on deferred projects. He said that there was a problem in Canada in connection with deferred municipal projects that could be of beneficial use to the general public. At the same time, he pointed out that there were large groups of unemployed in the country, and this legislation would bring these two things together and help both of the problems. No one could disagree with that, Mr, Chairman; that is a very desirable end result.
The minister also suggested that this measure would provide funds immediately and activate those deferred projects. Well, up to this point, Mr. Chairman, we have no disagreement. We agree with the aims and objectives. Then, the minister dealt with the conditions that were going to be attached, and to the techniques to be used, in getting
11, 1983	913
Municipal Development and Loan Board this money out to the municipalities so that they could make use of it. He said, of course, there would be forgiveness of a significant portion of the loan if certain conditions were met. One condition was that certain projects would be undertaken and completed by a certain date. He said that funds would be available only for additions to projects that were now under way. In other words, there would almost have to be an undertaking that the municipality had not previously considered, or at least had not initiated any action on it up to this point.
One other condition was that there was to be no interference with the ordinary financing of the municipalities, as they are doing it today. I suggest one of the major problems facing municipalities today is the tremendous capital costs and interest charges connected with the so-called ordinary financing. A number of references have been made during this debate to the fact that 30 per cent or 40 per cent of municipal budgets are being appropriated in order to pay interest on the debt the municipalities already have. We in this group had hoped that, finally, there was to be some action taken to relieve the municipalities of these tremendous charges for capital.
However, apparently the Minister of Finance is using this legislation as another means, if they want to call it that, of dealing with the unemployment problem. We do not disagree with that idea, that there is need for some action in respect of unemployment. But we also believe that this was an opportunity, and is an opportunity for that matter, to deal with the unemployment problem in the nation and at the same time relieve the municipalities of these tremendous debt charges which are becoming almost unbearable.
One of the other conditions to which the minister referred was that the rate of interest to be charged would be based on the federal government borrowing rate. The Minister of Finance is on record as being in favour of debt free money. I suggest to him that if he will apply this idea, that the charge to the municipalities will be equal to, or based upon, the federal government borrowing rate and then sell the bonds that are necessary to raise this $400 million to the Bank of Canada we would, in fact, achieve a lowering of the interest rate and pass on some very beneficial savings to the municipalities. The minister is in favour of this process, so I urge that he implement this idea, carry on with this technique, for obtaining the funds that are so badly needed to stimulate employment and help the municipalities with their deferred projects.

Then, Mr. Chairman, the minister moved on to the administrative aspects of this legislation. He suggested that the board be set up in conjunction with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Alberta are pretty heavily in debt.

speechtext: Yes, I am coming to that. I am glad you brought that up. I should like to outline for a few minutes the set-up in the province of Alberta which has proven so beneficial to the municipalities. As a matter of fact, I suggest that if all the provinces in Canada had a similar arrangement between the provincial government and municipalities as the one that exists in Alberta, many of the objections that have been raised by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue simply would not apply.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: You do not really believe that do you?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
For example, back in the early 50's the province of Alberta set up a municipal revolving fund to encourage municipalities to put in sewerage and water systems, and so on. Loans were made to municipalities at 2 per cent interest under what was called revolving self-liquidating loans. For a number of years the surpluses of the treasury of Alberta were sufficient to supply all the funds that were required under this measure to meet the demands of the municipalities for putting in sewerage systems, water systems and many other projects. I might say that this measure was so successful that almost all the towns and villages, somewhere around 98 per cent, with a population of over 100 have water and sewerage systems. As a matter of fact, in many cases after these projects were carried out unconditional grants were made by the province to the municipalities sufficient to cover the cost of repaying both the principal and the interest. But the other important feature of this kind of assistance to the municipalities is that the payments of both principal and interest go back into the fund so that the money can be used over and over again.


However, by about 1958 the demands from the municipalities were in excess of the amount of money that the province itself could put into the fund, and so a municipal finance corporation was set up. Under this arrangement the province borrows in lump sums all of the money that is required by all of the municipalities in the province of Alberta, and by doing so the province obtains this money at a substantially better rate of interest than if the municipalities had to go into the money market individually.
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance that here you have a tailor made scheme already in operation. The administrative requirements for what is probably anticipated in this resolution are already set up, so far as the province of Alberta is concerned. There will be no interference with provincial rights if the government will deal with the municipal finance corporation. On the other hand, if you set up another board, whether or not it is in conjunction with C.M.H.C., and try to deal directly with the municipalities I think you will run into some constitutional problems and perhaps bring about some disagreement with the province that really is not necessary.
Another point in the resolution now before us is that all of this money will be granted only if it is for programs in addition to those that are already taken care of by means of the usual and ordinary financing of programs that municipalities have been doing in the past. In dealing with the exemptions, the minister ruled out such things as hospitals, sewerage systems, capital needs for education, which I suppose means school buildings and all of the other facilities that are required for education. By these exemptions I think he took away at least half of the capital responsibilities of the municipalities.
What do we have left? We have streets and maybe some other local improvements. But what do you do in a case where a municipality thinks that expanding, improving and modernizing its educational facilities happens to be the most important project needed for that area? What if they are not willing to borrow money outside of the exemptions, with the strings that will be attached to it? I think there is a very real possibility that we will find situations where the municipal boards themselves feel that the modernizing of hospitals or educational facilities is paramount in their requirements. But if they are going to benefit from this legislation and stimulate employment, they will have to become involved in projects that are not as important. So, Mr. Chairman, I urge the minister to reconsider

some of these exemptions because I think there is a valid need to be a little less stringent in this regard.
I am more familiar, of course, with the province of Alberta than any other province, but I know that in all the other provinces as well there are bodies under the provincial governments that have a certain amount of control over municipalities within those provinces. I think most of them have regulations respecting the maximum amount of debt that a municipality can incur. Therefore I think that with respect to those provinces which do not already have a central borrowing agency, such as the municipal finance corporation of Alberta, it would be well for the Minister of Finance to encourage those provinces to set up some such body so that the most effective use can be made of whatever money is available and so that this can be done without getting into controversy with the provincial authorities.
Finally, I wish to repeat that we believe this resolution and the legislation to follow could provide an opportunity for the federal government to do something in a very positive way to relieve the municipalities of the tremendous debt charges that are becoming almost unbearable. I know we all realize that currency and credit are under the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government, and it is here that the government has authority to make changes in the monetary and fiscal system of the country. If we look into the future and take into consideration some of the figures that the minister himself projected before he was in the office he now holds, it is almost alarming when one realizes the tremendous debt service charges that are going to be piled upon municipal governments in the years to come. Certainly it seems to me that we should take full advantage of this opportunity to work out some kind of arrangement so that the capital requirements of the municipalities can be provided at a lower rate of interest.

Mr. Chairman, it is with some genuine satisfaction I rise to take part briefly in this debate and to commend the proposed legislation to the committee. The principle of the proposed legislation and its significance to our cities and towns have been described so ably by my colleague, the Minister of Finance, that my words may perhaps seem unnecessary. Nevertheless, I have more than an academic interest in the municipal development and loan act. It has already been made clear that, if and when the bill is passed, its various provisions will be implemented through established facilities of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As the minister responsible for the operations of the corporation I too will have a task to perform.
I am very happy with this turn of events. It seems to me the proposals being introduced today, together with certain amendments to the National Housing Act, I hope also to be given your early consideration, constitute a vigorous, two-pronged attack on some of the growth problems of our municipalities. Together they will answer an urgent need to boost the economy and to provide substantially increased employment.
I need hardly remind the committee that many Canadian cities are in a period of increased expansion. For better or for worse, therefore, important planning decisions are constantly being made by governments, institutions, firms and individuals. The nature and character of our living environment now and in the future, will reflect the wisdom of these decisions, in both small and large urban areas. Surely it is obvious that no area of public policy has a more lasting and pervasive effect on our well-being than the orderly, comprehensive development of our urban environment.
Our course of action then is clear. We must take positive, dynamic steps to improve our whole habitat, steps that will afford-at the same time and in one stroke-new impetus to the economy and more jobs for our people.
916	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Municipal Development and Loan Board
I submit the municipal development and loan act and the amended National Housing Act to be introduced, taken together and operating in concert, can and will achieve these ends. For some years from the opposition benches I have sought and asked that the fullest consideration be given by the federal government to measures of this kind.
I am now happy to be associated with such presentations to parliament for action.
In certain conditions, and these conditions certainly are with us today, the addition by the federal government of capital funds to the stream of resources available for proper urban growth, is a practical, desirable, forward-looking act. It is my opinion that the action is even more desirable when the funds are used for the highest and best social and economic purposes.
By this I do not wish for a moment to decry government investments for other purposes. They too are invariably imperative. They too give a fillip to the national economy and to the level of employment. But, are there not important advantages to be gained by earmarking more national investments for vital municipal projects that would not otherwise go forward. It is my feeling that, as a supplement to local capital expenditures already committed, and to provincial assistance to municipalities, such funds so invested will have a much more solid impact on growth and development and on expanded work opportunities. At the same time we will be helping our urban communities, large and small, to provide the services they so urgently require, encouraging them also to plan for the future with greater effect, and thereby creating a new and improved environment for our own and future generations.
That is what I mean by the highest and best purposes. I suggest that, viewed in this light, we can bring forward, with enthusiasm, this among the other legislative instruments proposed in the speech from the throne.
There will be those who ask bluntly; how many new jobs? I am not going to try my hand as a forecaster. I believe any such guess would be difficult because of the varied and almost incalculable effects that follow improvements in social capital, but I do draw the attention of committee members to one or two significant statistics.
Private and public expenditures on new construction are estimated for 1963 at $6,060 million. Forecast capital expenditures by all municipalities at $865 million represent more than 14 per cent of the total. I suggest it follows that the added incentives to municipalities proposed by my colleague, particularly if taken in conjunction with the N.H.A. amendments to which I have already referred, may call for a re-assessment of these figures.

There are those who are concerned about the constitutional aspects. Indeed the question has already quite properly been asked in the house. I need hardly repeat the assurance given by the Prime Minister recently during his address to the annual conference of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. He said, you will recall, that only those projects approved by the province concerned will qualify for loans, and in turn, for a partial rebate of the debt they incur. He also made it clear the proposed federal assistance "will not take away one shred of local autonomy."
May I conclude by saying that when the proposed legislation becomes law, I and the personnel, facilities and services of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are ready to implement a program of undeniable benefit, not only to Canada's municipalities now being cast in new moulds, but to the whole design and fabric of the nation itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, many hon. members, including a number of my colleagues in the New Democratic party, have had long experience in local government and are well aware of the problems to be faced. With the rapid increase in the growth of towns and cities since world war II there have been increasing demands on local authorities for more and better services. One has only to think of roads, sewers, water and lighting, as well as housing, health, education, recreation and planning. The demands are almost overwhelming.
One of the greatest difficulties is the confusion and indefiniteness that prevails regarding areas of responsibility. Local men are close at hand, and it is not surprising therefore that buck passing has become an accomplished art when capital cities are thousands of miles away from local areas. The provincial capitals and Ottawa have become the scapegoats of administrators on the local scene.
Clarification is needed among these three levels of government, and municipal authorities need broader bases of taxation. Land is no longer the sound criterion of ability to pay. Mr. Chairman, I would like to quote

from an editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 8 entitled "Whose hand in which pocket":
In Detroit representatives of Canadian municipalities discovered that many United States local governments have other sources of direct revenue than property or direct business taxes, such as personal income and sales taxes. Property owners in U.S. urban communities contribute only 46 per cent of the total tax revenue of cities, while in Canada they contribute more than 80 per cent.
There is a central theme to these various statements which has been sung in Canada of late. It is that in the ideal democratic community, each government, whether local, provincial or federal, has defined duties, defined sources of revenue, and accepts responsibility before the public for raising and spending its own taxes. If it errs the taxpayer knows precisely whom to blame.
In Canada this clear responsibility has become confused in a tremendously complicated jungle of grants, subsidies and hidden forms of taxation. The taxpayer does not know how much he pays in taxes or, in some cases, to which level of government he pays them. The politician, relieved of much direct responsibility for raising taxes, can, and often does, become correspondingly careless about the ways in which he spends them.
In the same issue, sir, there was an article entitled "B.C. professor backs new deal for Quebec". The article reads:
Donald V. Smiley, associate professor of political science at the University of British Columbia, said yesterday-
That is, he said this in a paper presented to the Canadian Political Science Association:
-the confederation agreement of 1867 should be revised to adapt it to the new needs and wants of all levels of government in 1963.
"From about the end of the first world war onward, Anglo-Canadians have come increasingly to look to Ottawa for leadership and money in respect to what are considered as worthy national purposes-
More recently, influential currents of thought and policy in Quebec have come to assert that an increasing range of autonomy in fiscal and economic matters is essential to the survival and expansion of French Canadian culture", he said.
Holding that Canadians must recognize that Quebec is not a province like the others, Dr. Smiley said that a reconciliation on constitutional problems is possible within the present federal framework.
"Its essential element would be a different sharing of legislative powers, revenue sources and functional responsibilities between Quebec and Ottawa than that which prevails between the federal government and those of the other provinces", he said.
Many areas will welcome the opportunity to borrow from this fund that we are now discussing if regulations regarding rates and requirements are attractive and clean-cut. If the means test is too demanding or too obscure, the most needy councils will bypass the federal offer. They will claim, and rightly so, that the uncontrolled sections of their budgets, resulting from previous borrowings, are already embarrassing and frustrating and leave them little room for manoeuvring or planning desirable improvements in their
11, 1963	917
Municipal Development and Loan Board districts. To be of advantage to local governments the write-offs or payments to be forgiven must not be vague or uncertain. Municipalities must know where they stand in regard to all these matters.
The winter works program will be needed to supplement projects financed under the loan fund, but I do suggest to the Minister of Labour that he should examine very carefully the regulations having to do with the winter works program and that he should consider including not only labour costs as a legitimate charge in this connection but also charges for engineering, planning, equipment and machinery. I saw many constituencies and municipalities which had difficulty in the past year or two qualifying under the regulations of the winter works program because of the heavy cost of engineering and equipment. I urge that those costs be included as legitimate charges in this program.
All employing agencies, both public and private, have a social obligation to maintain employment at a high level. We are concerned at the moment with the responsibility of the public sector of our economy. It is a major factor in the employment picture. Every modem government that has a heart views chronic unemployment as a social disease that will be removed only by bold and far reaching decisions. Measures announced so far fall far short of meeting this need. However, hon. members of this house will hope that all three levels of government in this country will combine to assure a substantial improvement in the employment situation during 1963.

We don't roll them up; we put snow on them. One of the earlier speakers talked about expressways through cities and suggested that cities would benefit through being able to build expressways. In Ontario, the provincial government makes a substantial grant toward the building of connecting highway links through municipalities. When a highway runs through a town or a city, the province assumes a substantial portion of the cost of construction. Will these projects be excluded from assistance under the program now proposed because the province participates financially?
The avowed purpose of this scheme is to provide employment, and everyone hopes it will do so. We hope it will provide employment in substantial quantities, particularly in winter. However, it seems to me that in introducing the resolution the minister put so many qualifications and hedges about it that it will not bring about these very laudable purposes. As a matter of fact, the resolution as introduced could perhaps best be described as niggardly in relation to providing against unemployment. Of course, it does not meet

the larger problem at all. I have in mind the question of the tax relationship between municipal, provincial and federal levels of government. Surely, if there is one problem which is disturbing confederation today, it is the one which has as its basis the financial relationship between the various levels of government. It would seem to me that if the intentions of the government were sincere this would have been a good place at which to begin tackling this question. It is no answer at all to provide another conditional grant- and that is all we are doing; we are providing another conditional grant which is hedged about with restrictions to an even greater degree than are most such grants. A few years ago, Ontario at least attempted to meet this problem head on by providing a per capita grant unconditionally to all the municipalities in the province. That was a direct attack on the system of government grants destroying municipal autonomy. But nothing at all has been said or done in this direction in the resolution now before us.
Nevertheless, while this is only a small crumb from the table, one can support the resolution, or one hopes one can support it, though with a substantial degree of misgiving.

speechtext:
Some of the previous speakers from the Conservative party and the Social Credit party have made a great deal of the constitutional question involved when the federal government enters into any kind of relationship with the municipalities. I think they are over-emphasizing this point. There is no great problem here. This matter has already arisen with regard to the winter works program, and in the section of the National Housing Act which provides for sewer lines, so I do not think there should be any particular problem in this direction. Moreover, the resolution states clearly that, in order to qualify, projects must meet with the approval of the province concerned.
I recall that during the election campaign the Liberal party stated that in order to bring about full employment and prosperity in Canada, both long term and short term measures were needed. The long term measures presumably include the setting up of bodies such as the economic council and the proposed department of industry. Spokesmen for the Conservative party stated, I think rightly, that it might be some time before the effects of such measures were felt. They also said that certain short term measures were necessary in order to provide work for the large numbers of people who were unemployed. The Minister of Finance recognized this need and mentioned it this afternoon, stating that the level of unemployment had been running at an average of 6.6 per cent in the last few years. He also recognized the
Municipal Developmeni and Loan Board needs of the municipalities, saying there was a backlog of capital works to be carried out.
I should like to submit that the proposed loan board and the amount of money suggested will not achieve satisfactorily the purposes the minister has in mind. Four hundred million dollars spread over three years will do some good; any aid to the municipalities will be appreciated, I am sure of that. Even the winter works program of the last few years, small as it was, did help. But if the government wishes to tackle the outstanding needs of the urban areas and if the minister really wishes to come to grips with the serious level of unemployment, the amount of money proposed here will not do the job. By way of illustration, the money provided in connection with the sewer loans amounts to $200 million over three years. Most of this is allocated at the present time. So I suggest that $400 million for all the municipalities of Canada over three years will not be very successful in coping with the situation.
I was sorry to hear the minister say that various types of public works are to be excluded from the benefits of this legislation. Hospitals are to be excluded, he says, because there is already some legislation which covers them. Schools are not to be included; sewers are not to be included, because provision is made for them under the terms of N.H.A. at the present time. I would add that only certain types of sewage works are included among the present N.H.A. legislation, which tends to concentrate on trunk lines. There is not much help for the general lateral lines serving the residential areas. So that if you take into account these exclusions, I think we have left the question of the roads, which is quite a big problem, and I think the city of Ottawa can probably use $50 million of that itself. There are also the sidewalks and possibly public buildings such as city halls and libraries. I think it would be of much more value if the lines could be widened, particularly the installation of sewer services, which is most expensive.
However, Mr. Chairman, the main point I am trying to make tonight, and it will not take very long to make it, is this. If the government intends to give the economy a shot in the arm to try to relieve unemployment quickly, they are thinking in terms of amounts too small for that purpose. I am sure that among government advisers both in parliament and outside there must be people who hold the same general economic views which are held by Dr. Samuelson of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and economic adviser to President Kennedy, views held by many Canadian economists. I am sure the Minister of Finance is aware of those views. The amount of money necessary, even
920	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board though large deficits would be incurred, is much greater than that proposed through the new loan board. As the legislation stands at the present time it will fail in the two purposes it has in mind. It will not do very much to get at the long deferred projects of our cities and municipalities, and it will not make that much difference to unemployment. I should like to think that the government will take another look at this and decide that the $400 million should be applied within a 12 or 18 month period instead of over a period of three years. To conclude, Mr. Chairman, any help which is given to the municipalities is welcome, but I submit that this measure will fail in its main purpose, which is to try to improve employment in Canada.

speechtext:
What appals me the most is to see the hon. members opposite applauding. What are they cheering about? What has the Liberal party done since it came to power?
On the evening of the fifty fourth day, we have witnessed a shameful attempt by the present government to violate the Canadian constitution.
This afternoon, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has explained the resolution now under study. According to him, that measure should be more than effective in dealing with unemployment. We all want to see the Canadian economy move forward and one can wonder if that measure, outside its constitutional aspect, really offers an effective remedy to the worsening unemployment situation in our country.
Up to now, it has been impossible to know whether the provinces have been consulted in regard to the act proposed in the resolution under study.
On May 20, 1963, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) asked the Minister of Justice whether he had consulted the provinces about this measure. As can be seen on page 38 of the official report, the Minister of Justice replied in these words:
Mr. Speaker, I am aware of no communication such as the one mentioned by the hon. member.
Mr. Chairman, will a member of the cabinet inform the committee of preliminary consultations which might have been entered upon between the provincial and federal authorities.
Someone may reply: We do not have to consult the provinces. We would then witness


an attempt to transgress the Canadian constitution as glaring as the one made by Messrs. St. Laurent and King when they were prime ministers.
Mr. Chairman, we must stop and ask ourselves under what power the present government intends to legislate in a field under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, since paragraph 8 of section 92 of the British North America Act says clearly that the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over the field of municipal legislation.
The present government asks us to pass a resolution that could unbalance existing legislation, especially in the province of Quebec.
1	do not know the municipal legislation systems of the other provinces, but in the province of Quebec, municipalities are governed by two special acts. First there is the cities and towns act, and then the municipal code which governs rural municipalities, township or parish municipalities. Those acts provide means of borrowing that are available to municipalities in order to carry out work under their jurisdiction. On the other hand, the proposal under study ignores legislative provisions, administrative rights that belong exclusively to the provinces.
Mr. Chairman, if we consider the resolution we read this:
That It is expedient to introduce a measure to promote increased employment in Canada by the provision of financial assistance by way of loans to municipalities-
Now if the primary purpose of the measure is to assist municipalities, and if the central government really wants to help the provinces, the Minister of Finance should allow the provinces to make a further deduction of
2	or 3 per cent on personal and corporate income taxes, which would result in an increase in the revenues of the provinces that would enable them to assist municipalities in the carrying out of their projects. By doing that, we would respect the Canadian constitution and we would not interfere with the rights of the provinces, as suggested by this resolution.
Under existing provincial legislation, municipalities wishing to borrow money must go on the market and ask for the required loan through the official gazette of Quebec. The organizations interested must tender in regard to the loans to municipalities and send their tenders to the municipalities within the period allowed previously in the regulations and stipulated in the notice.
Therefore, in order to comply with the provisions of existing municipal bylaws in the province of Quebec, the federal govern-

xnent should normally have to tender for loans to the municipalities of the province.
This is altogether inconsistent and illegal at the same time, because the federal government can in no way interfere with municipal administration.
The Minister of Finance said this afternoon that this legislation provides for a fund of $400 million to be made available to the C.M.H.C. and which will be administered by a board.
The board may well adopt administrative regulations or measures that would contradict the provisions of existing legislation in all provinces.
If such a thing happened, which legislation would have priority, the provincial laws concerning municipalities or the adminstrative regulations of the board?
Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that this resolution is dangerous and, as long as members of this house are not clearly informed as to any previous consultation with the provinces, we have no right to approve such an obvious interference of the federal government in a field of exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
If Ottawa truly wishes to help solve the unemployment problem, it can do so without violating the constitution and section 92 of the B.N.A. Act.
Furthermore, even if this legislation were constitutional, there is a strong possibility that it will benefit only the large metropolitan areas, because I do not feel that small municipalities will benefit from it. In my opinion, taxpayers will have to share in repaying the loans raised to carry out the work. Municipal councils will be forced to increase property taxes or to collect a special tax in order to meet their obligations when the loans fall due.
Where will the government borrow those $400 million it is ready to contribute? Let us hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in his budget speech next Thursday night will throw some light on this subject. The government will have to levy direct or indirect taxes in order to repay those loans obtained on the money market. However, it is again the Canadian taxpayer who will have to bear the burden resulting from the implementation of this act.
Mr. Chairman, the members from Quebec in this house would be interested to know

And if the province has been consulted, can we be sure that the existing legislation will be amended so that it would be in line with the wording of the act that will follow the adoption of this resolution?
Would it not be a good thing to ask the present government, which seems quite willing to help the provinces, to yield to the provinces the right to levy taxes strongly claimed by the premier of the province of Quebec, Mr. Jean Lesage? And the attitude taken by Quebec's premier is perfectly logical under the circumstances. I wonder how our hon. friends opposite, the members from the province of Quebec, will manage to support that resolution, when the premier of the province of Quebec, who backed them up in the last election campaign, has presented the federal government-whichever it was to be-with an ultimatum for the granting to the province of Quebec of 25 per cent of the personal income tax to be levied and 100 per cent of the succession duties.

Municipal Development and Loan Board perity and at last finding a solution to the unemployment problem. But what is much more important, Mr. Chairman, is to respect the Canadian constitution. I am quite sure that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Cantin) will bring enough pressure to bear on members of the cabinet for us to get the information we need before we are called upon to decide on the advisability of this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, since this is the first time you have been in the chair when I am on my feet, I take this opportunity to congratulate you on your appointment.
We are now wondering a lot about their proposed financial assistance to municipalities in the form of loans to reduce unemployment.
We are very happy that this resolution was submitted, but it remains to be seen whether we will be as pleased with the administration of the act.
First of all, we find there some of the ideas advocated for several years by our group about a municipal development bank. Even though that name is not given to the new organization, we hope that this was the minister's idea in moving this resolution.


Otherwise, we should be forced to agree with those who have doubts as to infringement of provincial jurisdiction.
If the minister wants to feed his $400 million fund which he needs to carry out this plan in the same way as the other parties do, there is no doubt that he will encroach upon provincial autonomy. As a matter of fact, he will have to delve deeply in the taxpayer's pocket and get three times as much as he will be able to pay out to the unemployed. Mind you, on the basis of what the Liberals said during the last election campaign, when speaking about the Social Credit, whenever the government gives you a dollar, it has levied three from the taxpayer.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, the provinces should have the right to levy their own taxes; they are now old enough to set up their own taxes; they hardly need to be shown the trick by the federal government.
Let us start by leaving the provinces their revenues. And you will be surprised to find that there are among those provincial legislators, men who are quite as qualified as the federal ones to spend their revenue in a judicious way.
The great principle to the effect that a right is attached to every duty is still true. If the municipalities have the obligation and the power, much more so than the federal government, to carry out such duty, if it is their duty to create a climate favourable to the development of their area, then the central government cannot take away from them the rights that are necessary to the fulfilment of their duty.
There is no end to recriminations about everything going wrong in Canada! Why? Because no one, beginning with the central government, is playing his own part. Because the strong still seek to displace the weak.
Do you not think we are going back to the law of the jungle? Everybody wants to interfere with other people's business and at the same time neglects his own business. While the provinces urge the central government to give them back the sources of income they had lent it when danger threatened, that same government, grateful as a lion, does not want to give back anything to those who came to his help. Far from giving them back their old taxation powers, the government does the utmost every day to find new devices to restrict a little more their freedom of action before choking them for good.

On the other hand, the provinces play the same game with the municipalities and school boards which they will control within a few years.
School boards are in urgent need of money; municipalities also need money. The provinces are hard put to find new sources of revenue. And, in the meantime, the central government takes over all the fields of taxation. The federal government grabs almost all the revenue in the country and then the funds are administered by a bureaucracy over which that same government has no control. And, in order to hide that inability, new boards, commissions and departments are set up. I feel that, under present conditions, we might as well grant the provinces what they want and give them back their whole taxation rights. Then they would solve themselves their own unemployment problem. But if the minister must set up a $400 million fund through the Bank of Canada, then there is nothing more to fear for provincial autonomy. Because this government will then simply authorize the Bank of Canada to place the said amount at the disposal of municipalities. Each municipality will be absolutely free in its operations, since each one of them knows best the projects to be carried out in the area and is in the best position to determine who needs work.
Thus, this government agency, the Bank of Canada, for once will play its real part, which is to create the necessary credit to promote the development of municipalities and, by doing that, to give jobs to the unemployed.
I think that, in so doing, the minister will serve the purpose he has set for himself, while protecting at the same time the autonomy of one and all provinces.

speechtext: It is possible that there will be some time between the conclusion of the speech of my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance on Thursday evening and ten o'clock, and the government would hope to use that time for the deliberations of the house, and not to adjourn.
Never on Sunday, anyway.
It being five minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
